title: How Many Wives and Concubines Did Solomon Really Have?
paragraphs:
How Many Wives and Concubines Did Solomon Really Have?
The King Who Had Everything… Except the One Thing That Could Have Saved Him
There are sins that happen in a single moment. Then there are sins that happen one compromise at a time.

King Solomon's tragedy was not that he suddenly woke up one morning and abandoned God. His downfall was slower than that. It was almost invisible. It looked wise. It looked successful. It even looked blessed.
And that's what makes his story so terrifying.
Because many of us are walking the same road without realizing it.
We imagine that if we had Solomon's wisdom, influence, wealth, opportunities, and favor, we would never drift from God.
Scripture tells a different story.
The Bible records in 1 Kings 11:3:
"He had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines. And his wives turned away his heart."
The Hebrew text says:
וַיְהִי־לוֹ נָשִׁים שָׂרוֹת שְׁבַע מֵאוֹת וּפִילַגְשִׁים שְׁלֹשׁ מֵאוֹת וַיַּטּוּ נָשָׁיו אֶת־לִבּוֹ
Vayehi-lo nashim sarot sheva me'ot u'pilagshim shlosh me'ot vayattu nashav et-libbo.
The phrase וַיַּטּוּ נָשָׁיו אֶת־לִבּוֹ (vayattu nashav et-libbo) literally means:
"His wives bent, inclined, or turned his heart away."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say they merely distracted him.
It does not say they simply influenced him.
It says they turned his very heart.
The Hebrew word לֵב (lev) means far more than emotions. In biblical thought, it refers to the center of one's will, desires, affections, thoughts, loyalties, and spiritual direction.
Solomon's greatest loss was never his kingdom.
It was his heart.
Why Did Solomon Have So Many Wives?
The answer surprises many readers.
Ancient kings often married foreign princesses to secure political alliances. Every marriage represented peace treaties, military cooperation, trade agreements, and international influence.
From the world's perspective...
Solomon looked brilliant.
From heaven's perspective...
He was slowly violating God's command.
Long before Solomon became king, God had already warned Israel.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
"And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away..."
The Hebrew reads:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Ve'lo yarbeh-lo nashim velo yasur levavo.
Literally:
"He must not multiply wives for himself, so that his heart will not turn away."
God did not forbid this because He wanted kings to have less happiness.
He forbade it because He knew the human heart better than humans do.
The command was protection.
Not restriction.
What Were Concubines?
Many modern readers confuse wives and concubines.
A wife entered into a recognized covenant marriage with legal rights and social standing.

A concubine also had an acknowledged relationship with the man but possessed fewer legal protections and lower social status. Children born through concubines were generally recognized but often had different inheritance rights depending on the circumstances.
Although Scripture records concubinage, recording something is not the same as approving it.
The Bible often describes human failure honestly without presenting it as God's ideal.
From the very beginning, God's design was clear.
Genesis says:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."

Jesus later quoted this passage in Matthew 19:4–6, reaffirming God's original intention for marriage as a lifelong covenant between one man and one woman. Scripture consistently presents this creation pattern as God's design, even while faithfully recording the failures of many biblical figures.
Solomon Didn't Fall Because of Women.
He fell because he loved something more than complete obedience.
That is an uncomfortable truth.
His marriages were symptoms.
The deeper disease was compromise.
At first, perhaps he justified just one political marriage.
Then another.
Then another.
Eventually seven hundred wives.
Three hundred concubines.
No one accidentally arrives there.
Sin rarely announces itself with fireworks.
It whispers.
"Just this once."
"This will help your career."
"This relationship is different."
"You deserve this."
"You can handle it."
Compromise always sounds reasonable before it becomes ruin.
The Saddest Verse in Solomon's Story
1 Kings 11:4 quietly says:
"For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father."
The phrase "not wholly true" comes from the Hebrew שָׁלֵם (shalem) meaning complete, whole, undivided, or fully devoted.
God was never asking Solomon for perfection.
He desired wholehearted devotion.
The greatest danger for believers today is often not open rebellion.
It is divided affection.
Jesus would later say:
"Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." (Matthew 6:21)
The battle has always been about the heart.
Yet Even Solomon's Failure Points Us to Jesus
This is where the story changes.
Solomon's life is not merely a warning.
It is a signpost.
He was called the wisest king.
Yet his wisdom could not save him.
He built the Temple.
Yet he could not cleanse his own heart.
He possessed unimaginable riches.
Yet wealth could not satisfy his soul.
He ruled a kingdom.
Yet he could not rule his own desires.
Another Son of David would come.
Not surrounded by hundreds of wives.
But surrounded by sinners.
Not seeking political alliances.
But reconciling enemies to God.
Not building a temporary temple.
But becoming the true Temple through His own body.
Not offering animal sacrifices.
But offering Himself.
Jesus Christ succeeded where Solomon failed.
The Greek of John 19:30 records Jesus' final declaration:
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai).
"It is finished."
More literally:
"It has been fully accomplished."
The work Solomon could never complete...
Jesus finished.
The obedience Solomon could never sustain...
Jesus fulfilled.
The righteousness Solomon could never achieve...
Jesus gives freely by grace to everyone who trusts in Him.
That is why our story is never ultimately about Solomon.
It is about Christ.
Solomon's life reminds us that wisdom alone cannot save us.
Knowledge cannot save us.
Success cannot save us.
Religion cannot save us.
Only Jesus Christ can.
Perhaps your compromises are hidden.
Perhaps they are public.
Perhaps your heart has slowly drifted while everyone still thinks you're doing fine.
The invitation of the Gospel remains the same.
Repent.
Return.
Receive the grace that Christ purchased at the cross.
Jesus does not merely forgive scandal.
He rewrites it.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.

If this article strengthened your faith, helped you understand God's Word more deeply, or reminded you that Christ alone is worthy of your whole heart, would you consider helping us spread biblical truth? Every share can place God's Word before someone who may desperately need it today.
Your testimony may encourage another believer who is quietly fighting the same battle.
Some people lose a kingdom long before anyone notices they first lost their heart.
